zh.q: 桌上摆着两套装置，为什么同一块锌片要试两次？
zh.concl: 左边这套是必修课做过的：一杯稀硫酸、两片金属、一根导线就有电流；右边这套多了一根盐桥，正是本节课要问的「为什么」。
points: 两套装置的区别只有两处：一杯酸还是两杯、盐桥插没插。
电流表是唯一能把「有没有电流」变成数的仪器（分度 0.1 mA）。
左边这套已经有读数，说明单液装置不是「错的」，只是有代价。

zh.q: 把两根导线夹上去，铜片上凭什么冒出气泡？
zh.concl: 电子由锌片通过导线流向铜片；溶液中的 H⁺ 从铜片获得电子被还原成氢原子，结合成 H₂ 从铜片上放出（教材原话）。
points: 断开导线时锌片冒气泡，是锌与稀硫酸直接反应，与导线无关。
接通后气泡跑到铜片上，说明电子确实经导线到了铜片。
锌片上还剩气泡，说明单液装置里化学能有一部分没走导线（第 4 步量化）。

zh.q: 电流表指针偏了，到底是电子在流还是电流在流？往哪边？
zh.concl: 电子流出的一极是负极（锌片被氧化），电子流入的一极是正极（铜片，H⁺ 在正极上被还原）；电流方向与电子运动方向相反（教材原话）。
points: 「负极」是按电子流出命名的，不是按电压高低命名的。
电流方向是历史约定的正电荷流向，所以与电子方向相反——每年都有人错在这里。
导线里只有电子在流，离子不走导线（第 7 步讲离子走哪条路）。

zh.q: 单液电池放着不管，电流为什么越来越小？
zh.concl: 这种原电池中氧化反应与还原反应并没有完全隔开，锌与其接触的稀硫酸发生反应，电流会逐渐衰减（教材原话）。
points: 衰减不是「电池没电了」，是锌被酸白白消耗掉了。
自放电的 70 % 不走导线，那部分化学能直接变成热，不做功。
双液同一时段读数纹丝不动，差别不在电极材料，而在「Zn 有没有和酸直接接触」。

zh.q: 换成两杯溶液、插上盐桥，为什么读数反而更大也更稳？
zh.concl: Zn 失去电子变成 Zn²⁺ 进入溶液，电子由负极经导线流向正极，正极一端的 Cu²⁺ 获得电子变成 Cu 沉积在铜片上（教材原话）。
points: 电压变高是因为正极换了半反应：从 H⁺/H₂（0 V）换到 Cu²⁺/Cu（+0.3419 V）。
锌片不再冒气泡，说明它不再和酸直接接触——单液的毛病被装置结构消除了。
铜片上出现的是铜（沉积），不是气泡，两者不要混。

zh.q: 只是抽走一根装着琼脂的管子，电流凭什么归零？
zh.concl: 从上述装置中取出盐桥，电流表的指针又回到零点，即电路中没有电流通过（教材原话）。
points: 闭合回路必须同时有电子导体（导线）和离子导体（溶液 + 盐桥）。
电池并没有坏：把盐桥插回去，开路电压仍是 1.10 V——断的是离子通路，不是电极。
盐桥里是 KCl 饱和溶液的琼脂，离子可在其中自由移动——它提供离子通路，不提供电子。

zh.q: 电子走导线，那溶液里的电谁来补？
zh.concl: 盐桥中的 Cl⁻ 移向 ZnSO₄ 溶液，K⁺ 移向 CuSO₄ 溶液，使氧化还原反应持续进行，锌铜原电池得以不断地产生电流（教材原话）。
points: 电子只在导线里走，离子只在溶液和盐桥里走，两条路互不串。
阳离子往正极一侧去（K⁺ 去 CuSO₄），阴离子往负极一侧去（Cl⁻ 去 ZnSO₄），两个方向相反。
盐桥补的是电荷平衡：没有它，一侧正电荷越积越多，反应就走不下去。

zh.q: 把溶液配浓一点，读数为什么会变大？
zh.concl: 浓度变大，溶液导电能力变强、电池内阻变小，所以同样电动势下电流更大；电动势由两极的反应物决定，不由溶液浓度决定。
points: 浓度改的是「路好不好走」（内阻），不是「推力有多大」（电动势）——前提是两池浓度相等、同时改，能斯特项相消；若只有一边变浓，电动势也会变。
电动势由两极的材料与反应物决定（教材：输出电能的能力取决于反应物的氧化还原能力）。
断开导线时电流为 0 而电动势仍读到 1.10 V（开路电压），说明「有电压」不等于「有电流」。

zh.q: 考核：把台面调成一台能稳定输出电流的锌铜原电池
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：把「两池分开、盐桥插好、导线接通、溶液够浓」四件事同时照顾好，电流才又大又稳。
points: 装置选双液：单液一开始就有 6.6–7.3 mA，但达不到 10.0 mA，而且会衰减。
盐桥与导线是两个独立的「通路」，缺一个电流就是 0。
浓度要够（≥ 0.50 mol/L），否则内阻拖住电流。

en.q: There are two setups on the bench. Why try the same zinc strip twice?
en.concl: The left setup is from the required course: one beaker of dilute sulfuric acid, two metal strips and a wire give a current; the right setup adds a salt bridge, which is the "why" this lesson asks about.
points: The two setups differ in just two ways: one beaker or two, and whether the salt bridge is in.
The ammeter is the only instrument that turns "is there a current" into a number (0.1 mA divisions).
The left setup already gives a reading, so the single-solution cell isn't "wrong"; it just has a cost.

en.q: Clip on the two wires. Why do bubbles appear on the copper strip?
en.concl: Electrons flow from the zinc strip through the wire to the copper strip; H⁺ in the solution takes electrons from the copper strip, is reduced to hydrogen atoms, which combine into H₂ released from the copper strip (textbook wording).
points: With the wires off, the bubbles on zinc come from zinc reacting directly with the acid, nothing to do with the wire.
Once connected, bubbles move to the copper strip, showing electrons really do reach the copper through the wire.
Bubbles remain on the zinc, showing that in the single-solution setup some chemical energy doesn't go through the wire (quantified in step 4).

en.q: The ammeter needle moved. Is it electrons or current that flows, and which way?
en.concl: The electrode electrons flow out of is the negative electrode (zinc, oxidized); the one they flow into is the positive electrode (copper, where H⁺ is reduced); current flows opposite to electron motion (textbook wording).
points: The "negative electrode" is named for electrons flowing out, not for having lower voltage.
Current direction is the historical convention for positive charge flow, so it's opposite to electron flow; people get this wrong every year.
Only electrons flow in the wire; ions don't travel through the wire (step 7 covers where ions go).

en.q: Leave a single-solution cell running. Why does the current keep falling?
en.concl: In this cell the oxidation and reduction aren't fully separated: zinc reacts with the dilute sulfuric acid it touches, and the current gradually decays (textbook wording).
points: The decay isn't "the battery ran flat"; zinc is being wasted by the acid.
The 70 % self-discharge doesn't go through the wire; that chemical energy becomes heat directly and does no work.
The two-solution reading doesn't budge over the same time; the difference isn't the electrode material but "whether Zn touches the acid directly".

en.q: With two beakers and a salt bridge, why is the reading both larger and steadier?
en.concl: Zn loses electrons and enters the solution as Zn²⁺; electrons flow from the negative electrode through the wire to the positive, where Cu²⁺ gains electrons and deposits as Cu on the copper strip (textbook wording).
points: The voltage is higher because the positive electrode uses a different half-reaction: from H⁺/H₂ (0 V) to Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.3419 V).
The zinc stops bubbling, showing it no longer touches acid directly: the setup's structure removes the single-solution flaw.
What appears on the copper strip is copper (a deposit), not bubbles; don't mix them up.

en.q: You only removed a tube of agar. Why does the current drop to zero?
en.concl: Remove the salt bridge from the setup and the ammeter needle returns to zero: no current flows in the circuit (textbook wording).
points: A closed circuit needs both an electronic conductor (the wire) and an ionic conductor (solution + salt bridge).
The cell isn't broken: put the salt bridge back and the open-circuit voltage is still 1.10 V. What broke was the ion path, not the electrodes.
The salt bridge holds agar made with saturated KCl solution, in which ions move freely: it provides an ion path, not electrons.

en.q: Electrons go through the wire, so who balances the charge in the solution?
en.concl: Cl⁻ in the salt bridge moves toward the ZnSO₄ solution and K⁺ toward the CuSO₄ solution, so the redox reaction keeps going and the zinc-copper cell keeps producing current (textbook wording).
points: Electrons travel only in the wire and ions only in the solution and salt bridge; the two paths never cross.
Cations move toward the positive side (K⁺ to CuSO₄), anions toward the negative side (Cl⁻ to ZnSO₄), in opposite directions.
The salt bridge maintains charge balance: without it, positive charge would pile up on one side and the reaction would stall.

en.q: Why does the reading go up when you make the solutions more concentrated?
en.concl: Higher concentration makes the solution conduct better and lowers the cell's internal resistance, so the same EMF gives more current; the EMF is set by the electrode reactants, not the solution concentration.
points: Concentration changes "how easy the path is" (internal resistance), not "how hard it pushes" (EMF). This assumes both beakers have equal concentrations changed together, so the Nernst terms cancel; if only one side gets more concentrated, the EMF changes too.
The EMF is set by the electrode materials and reactants (textbook: the ability to deliver electrical energy depends on the reactants' redox ability).
With the wires disconnected the current is 0 but the EMF still reads 1.10 V (open-circuit voltage): "there's a voltage" doesn't mean "there's a current".

en.q: Assessment: set up the bench as a zinc-copper cell that delivers a steady current
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: only by handling all four at once (separate beakers, salt bridge in, wire connected, solution concentrated enough) is the current both large and steady.
points: Choose two solutions: one solution starts at 6.6–7.3 mA but can't reach 10.0 mA, and it decays.
The salt bridge and the wire are two separate "paths"; missing either one makes the current 0.
The concentration must be high enough (≥ 0.50 mol/L), or internal resistance holds the current back.
